title: One algorithm in a table, diagram and code
goal: Keep requirements, decision order and executable branches consistent on concrete inputs.

prerequisites.text: You understand inputs, outputs and conditional decisions.
C++ syntax is introduced within the examples.

sections.title: Different representations expose different concerns
paragraphs: Consider classifying an integer as negative, zero or positive. In natural language it seems obvious, but we might forget the zero case when implementing it.
A decision table enumerates all cases, pseudocode shows the evaluation order, a flowchart makes branches visible and C++ implements the transitions.
You are given the request “print the sign of a number.” Before writing if, agree on what zero means and what happens if reading fails. Carry those decisions into every representation.

sections.title: Decision tables test completeness
paragraphs: Write the conditions x<0, x==0 and x>0, each with one expected action. This reveals omitted or overlapping cases before code is written.
If a valid input does not belong to any row, the requirement is incomplete. For a sign classifier, the zero row is essential.
If two rows can match the same input, specify priority or make the conditions disjoint. Here the sign of the number picks exactly one row.

sections.title: Pseudocode makes the sequence explicit
paragraphs: A clear version reads: IF x<0 print negative; ELSE IF x==0 print zero; ELSE print positive. The logic can be reviewed by someone who does not yet know iostream.
Pseudocode conventions vary. Always state inputs, outputs and nesting unambiguously; pseudocode itself is not executable C++.

diagram.caption: Sign classifier pseudocode
diagram.text:
read x
if reading fails → invalid and stop
if x < 0 → negative
else if x = 0 → zero
else → positive

sections.title: Flowcharts visualize control flow
paragraphs: An oval commonly denotes start/end, a rectangle an action, and a diamond a condition. Arrows indicate the next step, with true/false paths labeled.
A flowchart is only useful if a reader can follow every input to the correct output. Unlabeled branches or arrows are a source of confusion.
For x=0 the first decision is no and the second is yes. If we drop the second decision, zero silently falls into the positive branch.

diagram.caption: Paths after successful input
diagram.text:
◇ x < 0?
├─ yes → [negative] → end
└─ no  → ◇ x = 0?
          ├─ yes → [zero] → end
          └─ no  → [positive] → end

sections.title: Code is a concrete implementation
paragraphs: Compare each pseudocode condition with the corresponding C++ branch. The remainder operator % is commonly used to test parity through x%2==0.
Check x=-5, x=0 and x=7. Equal observed results across these examples support consistency, though finite tests do not prove all possible cases.
Parity is a different requirement. For −5 the remainder after dividing by 2 is nonzero, so the result is odd. Testing oddness need not assume that the remainder always equals 1.

sections.title: From the decision table to code
paragraphs: Zero often falls through a verbal rule about positive and negative numbers. Take input 0 and trace both checks.
Predict one output line before running. Then compare it with the table and flowchart.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: The sign table has three rows: x<0 → negative; x=0 → zero; x>0 → positive. They are mutually exclusive and cover the allowed integers. C++ uses == for equality and = for assignment. An if / else if / else chain selects one branch. Three independent if statements need a separate condition audit and are not always equivalent.
Find the two lines containing if in the code. Locate the input failure check and explain why zero produces exactly one line.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

sections.title: Try a separate task
paragraphs: Classify temperatures from −50 to 50 inclusive. Print cold below 10, comfortable from 10 to 25 inclusive and hot above 25. Reject other or unreadable input as invalid. Make a decision table, pseudocode and a flowchart before implementation.
Predict the first case and one boundary case. Practice has a separate starter. After running it, explain which check or operation produced each result.

selfcheck.prompt: Trace the checks for x = −5. What is printed?
feedback: Yes. The first test is true, so later branches are skipped.
The x == 0 test does not match −5.
The final else is reached only after both tests are false.

execution.label: predict

selfcheck.prompt: What does a decision table help reveal?
options: It translates the text to C++
selfcheck.feedback: It exposes omitted or contradictory cases.

selfcheck.prompt: What shape commonly represents a condition in a flowchart?
selfcheck.feedback: A diamond denotes a decision and its alternative paths.

selfcheck.prompt: Can a C++ compiler execute pseudocode unchanged?
options: No, it needs a concrete implementation
selfcheck.feedback: Pseudocode is a description rather than valid C++ source.

selfcheck.prompt: Where does 25 go if the middle row says 10 ≤ temperature < 25 and the hot row still says temperature > 25? How should the code express your decision?
selfcheck.feedback: Name the paths for 10 and 25 in each representation and explain why both print comfortable.

practice.title: Three temperature bands
practice.task: Classify temperatures from −50 to 50 inclusive. Print cold below 10, comfortable from 10 to 25 inclusive and hot above 25. Reject other or unreadable input as invalid. Make a decision table, pseudocode and a flowchart before implementation.
criteria: The three ranges together cover every valid integer.
Name the paths for 10 and 25 in each representation and explain why both print comfortable.
practice.hint: Take 9, 10, 25 and 26. Each input must match exactly one row.

steps.action: Write the ranges and boundary inputs.
Transfer the conditions and actions into pseudocode and the flowchart.
Implement the branches and compare each run with the table.

terms.definition: A readable description of algorithmic steps without a single language's concrete syntax.
A table pairing relevant conditions with their expected actions.
A diagram of actions and branches linked by directed connections.
A record of the evolving program state through execution steps.
